subject: chemistry

items.q: Which statement describes what makes a reaction a reversible reaction?
items.correct: The products of the reaction can react to make the original reactants
items.misconception: The reaction runs fully forwards and then runs fully backwards again
items.why: Everyday reversible things are sequential - a swing goes out and then comes back, a video plays and then rewinds - so students import that one-then-the-other picture into chemistry. The specification says the products of the reaction can react to produce the original reactants. That is possible from the moment any product exists, so both changes can be happening in the same mixture at the same time.
items.random_wrong: The reaction ends with equal amounts of reactants and products

items.q: A reversible reaction is represented as A + B ⇌ C + D. What does this representation tell you about C and D?
items.correct: They can react together to form A and B again under the right conditions
items.misconception: They are products of the equation and so can never act as reactants
items.why: Students are taught to read equations left to right from the very beginning, and a reversible reaction is the first time that rule stops being the whole story. The ⇌ symbol shows two reactions. Read left to right, A and B are the reactants; read right to left, C and D are the reactants. Which substances are the reactants depends on which of the two reactions you mean.
items.random_wrong: They are formed completely first and then break down to give A and B

items.q: A reversible reaction is currently going in the forward direction. How could it be made to go in the reverse direction?
items.correct: By changing the conditions, for example by cooling it instead of heating
items.misconception: It cannot be changed once the forward reaction has already started off
items.why: Almost every reaction met before this point is treated as one-way, and irreversible examples such as burning are used so often that irreversibility feels like a rule about all reactions. For a reversible reaction the direction is not fixed by the reaction, it is fixed by the conditions. Changing the conditions, for example heating instead of cooling, changes which direction the reaction goes in.
items.random_wrong: By waiting, because a reversible reaction turns round by itself at the end

items.q: Ammonium chloride is heated at the bottom of a test tube: NH4Cl ⇌ NH3 + HCl. A white solid forms on the cool upper part of the tube. Why?
items.correct: The cooler conditions let ammonia and hydrogen chloride react together again
items.misconception: The solid melted, travelled up the tube as a vapour and then set again
items.why: The observation - solid disappears at the hot end, identical solid appears at the cool end - looks exactly like sublimation, and no new substance is visible in between. The change is chemical: ammonium chloride ⇌ ammonia + hydrogen chloride. Heating breaks it into two different gases, and the reverse reaction between those gases makes ammonium chloride again on the cool glass.
items.random_wrong: The forward reaction has now finished, so the reverse reaction can begin

items.q: The forward reaction of a reversible reaction is exothermic. What can be said about the reverse reaction?
items.correct: It is endothermic, and transfers the same amount of energy
items.misconception: It is exothermic too, because reactions release energy
items.why: Most reactions students meet and remember - burning, neutralisation, metal with acid - are exothermic, so 'reactions give out heat' becomes a general rule in their minds. If a reversible reaction is exothermic in one direction, it is endothermic in the opposite direction. Making the bonds that the forward reaction broke must take in the energy that breaking them released.
items.random_wrong: It is endothermic, but transfers less energy than the forward

items.q: In a reversible reaction the forward reaction transfers 176 kJ of energy to the surroundings. What happens in the reverse reaction?
items.correct: 176 kJ is taken in from the surroundings
items.misconception: Less than 176 kJ is taken in from them
items.why: Students correctly learn that energy is wasted in machines and in energy transfer chains, and carry that idea across to the energy change of a reaction, which is a fixed quantity. The specification is precise here: if a reversible reaction is exothermic in one direction it is endothermic in the opposite direction, and the same amount of energy is transferred in each case.
items.random_wrong: 176 kJ is given out to the surroundings

items.q: Blue hydrated copper sulfate is heated and turns into white anhydrous copper sulfate and water. This change is endothermic. What happens when water is added to the white solid?
items.correct: It turns blue and the mixture warms up, as energy is released
items.misconception: It turns blue and the mixture cools down, as energy is taken in
items.why: The heating step is the memorable, visible one in the lesson, and students assume that anything you do to this substance needs energy supplying. Heating hydrated copper sulfate is the endothermic direction. The opposite direction, adding water back, must therefore be exothermic, and it transfers the same amount of energy out again.
items.random_wrong: It stays white, because this change cannot be reversed again

items.q: A reversible reaction in a sealed flask has reached equilibrium. What is happening in the flask?
items.correct: The forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate
items.misconception: Both the forward and the reverse reactions have stopped happening
items.why: 'Nothing is changing' is read as 'nothing is happening'. Students have no way of seeing particles reacting, so a constant appearance is taken to mean a finished reaction. Equilibrium is reached when the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate. They are both still going; each one replaces exactly what the other removes, so no change can be observed.
items.random_wrong: Equal amounts of both reactants and products are now present in it

items.q: Why must a reversible reaction be carried out in apparatus which prevents the escape of reactants and products if equilibrium is to be reached?
items.correct: A substance that escapes cannot react back, so the rates never become equal
items.misconception: It makes no real difference; equilibrium is reached in any container eventually
items.why: Students think of equilibrium as something that happens with time rather than something that depends on nothing being lost from the mixture. If a product escapes it cannot take part in the reverse reaction, so the reverse reaction can never match the forward one and the forward reaction simply continues. The specification requires apparatus which prevents escape.
items.random_wrong: Both of the reactions stop as soon as any substance escapes from the flask

items.q: A mixture at equilibrium in a sealed flask is left for a further hour with the conditions unchanged. What happens during that hour?
items.correct: Nothing appears to change, but both reactions continue at equal rates
items.misconception: Nothing appears to change, because both of the reactions have stopped
items.why: 'Nothing is changing' is read as 'nothing is happening'. Students have no way of seeing particles reacting, so a constant appearance is taken to mean a finished reaction. Equilibrium is reached when the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate. They are both still going; each one replaces exactly what the other removes, so no change can be observed.
items.random_wrong: The amounts slowly become equal to each other as the mixture stands

items.q: What determines the relative amounts of reactants and products present at equilibrium?
items.correct: The conditions the reaction is carried out under
items.misconception: The big numbers in the balanced symbol equation
items.why: Balanced equations are used throughout chemistry to work out amounts, so students expect them to give the equilibrium amounts too. The equation gives the ratio in which substances react, not the amounts left at equilibrium. The relative amounts of all the reactants and products at equilibrium depend on the conditions of the reaction.
items.random_wrong: Nothing, since the amounts are always equal there

items.q: A system at equilibrium has one of its conditions changed. How does the system respond?
items.correct: It shifts in the direction that counteracts the change made
items.misconception: It cancels the change so that nothing is different at all
items.why: The word 'counteract' is heard as 'cancel', and Le Chatelier's Principle is often summarised in class as the system 'opposing' the change, which sounds total. The system responds to counteract the change, which means it shifts in the direction that opposes it. If it undid the change entirely, changing the conditions could never change the yield, and it clearly does.
items.random_wrong: It stops reacting until the original conditions come back

items.q: Le Chatelier’s Principle is used to make predictions about systems at equilibrium. What does it allow you to predict?
items.correct: Which way the position of equilibrium moves when a condition is changed
items.misconception: How much faster a reaction goes when one of the conditions is changed
items.why: Equilibrium is taught straight after rates of reaction, so temperature, pressure and concentration are already firmly attached in students' minds to speed rather than to yield. Le Chatelier's Principle is about the position of equilibrium, that is, the relative amounts present once equilibrium is reached again. It says nothing about how long that takes.
items.random_wrong: How long a reversible reaction takes to reach equilibrium in the first place

items.q: In the equilibrium 2NO2 ⇌ N2O4 the forward reaction is exothermic. The mixture is cooled. Using Le Chatelier’s Principle, what is the effect?
items.correct: The equilibrium shifts towards N2O4, so more N2O4 is present
items.misconception: The equilibrium shifts towards NO2, so more NO2 is present
items.why: Students link the word 'heating' to the word 'exothermic' because both involve heat, and pair the terms rather than thinking about which change opposes what was done. The system counteracts the change. Raising the temperature is counteracted by the direction that takes energy in, the endothermic one; lowering it is counteracted by the direction that gives energy out, the exothermic one.
items.random_wrong: The reaction slows down but the amounts present stay the same

items.q: Extra A is added to a system at equilibrium: A + B ⇌ C + D. Which concentrations change before equilibrium is reached again?
items.correct: The concentrations of all four of the substances change
items.misconception: Only the concentration of A changes, because A was added
items.why: Students treat the four substances as separate stores rather than as one linked system, so a change made to one is expected to stay with that one. The system is no longer at equilibrium, so both reactions adjust: the concentrations of all the substances will change until equilibrium is reached again. A falls back somewhat, B falls, C and D rise.
items.random_wrong: Only the concentrations of C and D change, and not A and B

items.q: In the equilibrium A + B ⇌ C + D, the concentration of B is increased. What happens next?
items.correct: More C and D are formed until equilibrium is reached again
items.misconception: More A and B are formed, as that side has more in it now
items.why: 'Shifts towards' is misread as 'moves to where the extra material is', instead of as the direction in which the system reacts to remove it. The system responds to counteract the change. The way to counteract extra reactant is to use some of it up, so the forward reaction runs further and more products are formed.
items.random_wrong: The extra B is used up entirely and nothing else changes

items.q: Product C is continuously removed from the equilibrium A + B ⇌ C + D. What is the effect on the system?
items.correct: More A and B react together, so more C and D are formed
items.misconception: The reaction stops, because C is needed for it to continue
items.why: Removing something feels like taking away a resource, and students think of the products as being needed to keep the reverse reaction, and therefore the equilibrium, going. If the concentration of a product is decreased, more reactants will react until equilibrium is reached again. Removing a product is a way of making more product form, not of stopping the reaction.
items.random_wrong: The equilibrium moves towards A and B, so less C is made

items.q: For H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI at equilibrium, extra H2 is added. When equilibrium is reached again, the concentration of HI is higher and that of I2 is lower. What does this show?
items.correct: Increasing a reactant caused more product to be formed
items.misconception: Increasing a reactant caused more reactant to be formed
items.why: 'Shifts towards' is misread as 'moves to where the extra material is', instead of as the direction in which the system reacts to remove it. The system responds to counteract the change. The way to counteract extra reactant is to use some of it up, so the forward reaction runs further and more products are formed.
items.random_wrong: Adding H2 changed the concentration of H2 and nothing else

items.q: The forward reaction of N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2 is endothermic. The temperature of the equilibrium mixture is increased. What happens to the amount of NO2?
items.correct: It increases, because a temperature rise favours the endothermic reaction
items.misconception: It decreases, because a temperature rise favours the exothermic reaction
items.why: Students link the word 'heating' to the word 'exothermic' because both involve heat, and pair the terms rather than thinking about which change opposes what was done. The system counteracts the change. Raising the temperature is counteracted by the direction that takes energy in, the endothermic one; lowering it is counteracted by the direction that gives energy out, the exothermic one.
items.random_wrong: It stays the same, because temperature changes only affect the rates

items.q: The forward reaction of 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3 is exothermic. The temperature of the equilibrium mixture is increased. What happens to the relative amount of SO3?
items.correct: It decreases, because the endothermic reverse reaction is favoured
items.misconception: It increases, because a higher temperature always gives more product
items.why: In rates work, raising the temperature always speeds a reaction up, and speed is easily confused with how far a reaction goes. Raising the temperature increases the relative amount of products for an endothermic reaction, but decreases it for an exothermic one. Whether the yield rises or falls depends on the energy change of the forward reaction.
items.random_wrong: It increases, because heating favours the exothermic forward change

items.q: The forward reaction of H2 + CO2 ⇌ CO + H2O is endothermic. The temperature of the equilibrium mixture is decreased. What happens to the amount of CO?
items.correct: It decreases, because cooling favours the exothermic reverse reaction
items.misconception: It increases, because cooling favours the endothermic forward reaction
items.why: Students link the word 'heating' to the word 'exothermic' because both involve heat, and pair the terms rather than thinking about which change opposes what was done. The system counteracts the change. Raising the temperature is counteracted by the direction that takes energy in, the endothermic one; lowering it is counteracted by the direction that gives energy out, the exothermic one.
items.random_wrong: It stays the same, because cooling only slows the two reactions down

items.q: The forward reaction of 2NO2 ⇌ N2O4 is exothermic. The flask is placed in iced water. What happens to the relative amount of N2O4?
items.correct: It increases, because cooling favours the exothermic forward reaction
items.misconception: It decreases, because cooling favours the endothermic reverse reaction
items.why: Students link the word 'heating' to the word 'exothermic' because both involve heat, and pair the terms rather than thinking about which change opposes what was done. The system counteracts the change. Raising the temperature is counteracted by the direction that takes energy in, the endothermic one; lowering it is counteracted by the direction that gives energy out, the exothermic one.
items.random_wrong: It decreases, because cooling always reduces the yield of a product

items.q: The percentage yield of product Z at equilibrium is 68% at 200 °C, 45% at 300 °C and 27% at 400 °C. What does this show about the forward reaction?
items.correct: It is exothermic, since raising the temperature lowers the yield
items.misconception: It is endothermic, since raising the temperature lowers the yield
items.why: Students link the word 'heating' to the word 'exothermic' because both involve heat, and pair the terms rather than thinking about which change opposes what was done. The system counteracts the change. Raising the temperature is counteracted by the direction that takes energy in, the endothermic one; lowering it is counteracted by the direction that gives energy out, the exothermic one.
items.random_wrong: It is exothermic, since raising the temperature speeds it up more

items.q: In the gaseous equilibrium N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3 the pressure is increased. Which way does the equilibrium position shift?
items.correct: Towards NH3, the side with the smaller number of molecules
items.misconception: Towards N2 and H2, the side with the larger number of them
items.why: Pressure is associated with 'more gas', so students expect a pressure rise to push the system towards whichever side has more gas molecules on it. An increase in pressure causes the equilibrium position to shift towards the side with the smaller number of molecules. Fewer gas molecules in the same space is what reduces, and so counteracts, the raised pressure.
items.random_wrong: Neither way, as the number of atoms is the same on each side

items.q: In the gaseous equilibrium N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2 the pressure is decreased. What is the effect on the equilibrium position?
items.correct: It shifts towards NO2, the side with the larger number of molecules
items.misconception: It shifts towards N2O4, the side with the smaller number of molecules
items.why: Pressure is associated with 'more gas', so students expect a pressure rise to push the system towards whichever side has more gas molecules on it. An increase in pressure causes the equilibrium position to shift towards the side with the smaller number of molecules. Fewer gas molecules in the same space is what reduces, and so counteracts, the raised pressure.
items.random_wrong: It does not shift, but the yield of NO2 falls as the pressure falls

items.q: All the substances in H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI are gases. The yield of HI at equilibrium is the same at 1 atm, 10 atm and 50 atm. Why does pressure have no effect here?
items.correct: The symbol equation shows two molecules on each side of it
items.misconception: Raising the pressure should raise the yield, so the data are wrong
items.why: Industrial chemistry is usually met through the Haber process, where high pressure does raise the yield, and that single case is generalised into a rule. The direction of the shift is decided by the numbers of molecules in the symbol equation. If the product side has more molecules the yield falls, and if both sides have the same number the pressure makes no difference.
items.random_wrong: The equation has the same number of atoms on each side of it

items.q: At equilibrium, are the amounts of reactants and products equal?
items.correct: Not usually. Equal rates are required, not equal amounts.
items.misconception: Equilibrium means the reactants and the products are present in equal amounts - that is what the word balance means.
items.why: The everyday sense of 'equilibrium' and 'balance' is equality of the two sides, and diagrams of see-saws and balances are used to introduce the word. The specification defines equilibrium by the rates: it is reached when the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate. The relative amounts of reactants and products depend on the conditions and are usually not equal.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How do you decide which side of a gaseous equation has fewer molecules?
items.correct: Count the molecules, using the big numbers in front of the formulae in the balanced equation.
items.misconception: Count the atoms on each side; the side with fewer atoms is the side the equilibrium shifts to at high pressure.
items.why: Balancing equations trains students to count atoms, and that habit is applied here even though a balanced equation always has equal numbers of atoms on both sides. A balanced equation has the same number of atoms on both sides by definition, so counting atoms can never distinguish them. Pressure depends on the number of molecules: in N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3 that is four on the left and two on the right.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.6.2 Reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium
